title: Sanya Malhotra's Matcha Tiramisu Recipe Puts a Japanese-Indian Twist on the Italian Classic
excerpt: The actress teamed up with content creator Omkar Pawar to swap coffee for matcha in a layered tiramisu that takes under 30 minutes to assemble.
body:
• Actress Sanya Malhotra collaborated with content creator Omkar Pawar to make a matcha-infused version of tiramisu.
  • The recipe replaces espresso with whisked matcha and uses cream cheese and cream for the filling, with ladyfingers as the base.
  • Matcha tiramisu requires no baking and can be assembled in under 30 minutes, making it a practical dessert for entertaining.

Matcha has been steadily gaining ground in India, showing up in lattes, smoothie bowls, and ice cream. Actress Sanya Malhotra just pushed it into dessert territory with a tiramisu matcha recipe she made alongside content creator Omkar Pawar, as featured on NDTV Food.

The Recipe

The process follows the bones of a classic tiramisu but swaps out espresso for matcha at every step. Here is how Malhotra and Pawar assembled it:

  1. Whisk cream cheese and cream together until the mixture turns soft and smooth.
  2. In a separate bowl, add three to four servings of matcha powder to a small amount of water. Whisk using a traditional matcha whisk until frothy.
  3. Dip ladyfingers into the prepared matcha liquid — quickly, so they absorb flavor without getting soggy.
  4. Arrange the matcha-soaked ladyfingers in a container, then spread the cream cheese mixture evenly over the top.
  5. Repeat the layers: more matcha ladyfingers, more cream filling.
  6. Dust the top with matcha powder, the same way coffee is sprinkled over a classic tiramisu.

One improvisation: the pair realized mid-recipe they had forgotten vanilla essence and substituted vanilla instant matcha instead, which Malhotra said added a subtle sweetness to the overall flavor.

"I cannot wait to make this for my friends. Ab koi bahana nahi chalega — try karo and enjoy karo."

— Sanya Malhotra

Why Matcha Tiramisu Works

Tiramisu's structure — alternating layers of soaked biscuit and creamy filling — adapts well to flavor swaps because the technique stays the same. Matcha's earthy bitterness plays a similar role to espresso, cutting through the richness of the cream cheese filling. The green color also makes for a more visually striking dessert than the brown-and-white original.

The recipe requires no baking, no oven, and no specialized equipment beyond a whisk. That makes it practical for home cooks who want an impressive-looking dessert without a complicated process.

The Matcha Moment in India

Matcha is still relatively new to the Indian market compared to its near-ubiquity in Japan, the US, and parts of Europe. But cafés in Mumbai, Delhi, and Bengaluru have been adding matcha drinks to their menus at a steady pace, and Instagram food creators have helped normalize it beyond the wellness-influencer niche. Malhotra's recipe gives it another push — this time into the home kitchen.
